question: A 19-year-old male with 1-week frontal sinusitis develops increasing periorbital swelling, proptosis, restricted and painful extraocular movements, and visual acuity falling to 6/60 in the right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis and the correct immediate management?

answers.text: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis — treat with IV antibiotics and reassess in 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Preseptal cellulitis does not cause proptosis, restricted eye movements, or visual loss. This presentation is far more advanced.

answers.text: Orbital cellulitis without abscess — treat with IV antibiotics alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Orbital cellulitis without abscess is treated medically, but visual loss and restricted motility indicate the more severe stage requiring imaging to exclude abscess.

answers.text: Orbital (subperiosteal or intraorbital) abscess — emergency surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia, and falling visual acuity indicate an orbital abscess (Chandler stage IV-V). Threatened vision is an ophthalmic emergency requiring CT orbit and emergency surgical drainage combined with IV antibiotics.

answers.text: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — anticoagulation plus IV antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents bilaterally with high fever, severe headache, and meningism — not a unilateral orbital abscess picture. This patient needs orbital drainage first.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review Chandler's classification of orbital complications of sinusitis. Proptosis + restricted painful eye movements + visual loss = orbital abscess, requiring emergency surgical decompression, not antibiotics alone.

Excellent. Falling visual acuity in a patient with sinusitis and orbital signs is an emergency. Orbital abscess (Chandler IV) requires urgent CT and surgical drainage — delay risks permanent blindness.
